title: Working a foundation chain
subtitle: Counting, tension, and the turning chain
excerpt: The foundation chain is the starting row most flat crochet is built on. Getting it the right length, even, and not too tight saves trouble in every row above it. This covers counting chains, keeping the tension loose, and when to add a turning chain.
sourceNotes: Reconstructed in our own words from Thérèse de Dillmont, Encyclopaedia of Needlework (1886), Chapter 9 (Crochet Work), the passages on the chain stitch and working the first row into it (Fig. 403 and Fig. 414). Public domain via Project Gutenberg.

glossaryTerms.definition: The starting row of chain stitches that the first row of a flat piece is worked into. Its length sets the width of the work.
One or more chains worked at the start of a row to lift the hook to the height of the first stitch. A double crochet takes one, a treble takes three.
The simplest crochet stitch, made by drawing the yarn through the loop on the hook. A run of chains makes the foundation.

content.text: The
foundation chain
is the row of
chains

that most flat crochet starts from. The first row of real stitches is worked into it, so its length sets the width of the piece, and its tension sets how easily that first row goes in. A chain that is even and a touch loose makes everything above it easier.
What you need
A ball of smooth DK yarn in a light colour, so the chains are easy to count while you learn.
A 4 mm crochet hook, the standard pairing for DK.
A stitch marker or a scrap of contrast yarn to mark every tenth chain on a long foundation.
How to do it
Make a slip knot and place it on the hook.
Wrap the yarn over the hook and draw it through the loop to make the first chain. Repeat until you have the number the pattern calls for.
Count the V shapes along the front as you go. Do not count the slip knot, and do not count the loop on the hook.
Add the
turning chains
the pattern asks for. Work one extra chain for a first row of double crochet, or three for a first row of treble.
Check the tension by sliding the hook back through a chain. If it drags, the chain is too tight; start again one hook size larger for the chain only.

You will know the chain is right when it lies flat without twisting, the loops are even, and the hook slides into each one without a fight. Once the first row is worked the chain should not pull or pucker the edge.
Common mistakes
Chaining too tightly. This is the most common fault and it makes the first row hard to work and the bottom edge pull in. Keep the chain loose, or go up a hook size for it.
Miscounting. A foundation one chain short or long throws the whole pattern. Mark every tenth chain so a recount is quick.
Counting the turning chains as part of the stitch count when the pattern lists them separately. Read whether the pattern includes them or not before you start.
When to use it

Use a foundation chain to start any flat piece worked in rows: scarves, dishcloths, blankets, edgings worked lengthways. Pieces worked in the round usually start from a magic ring instead, and stretchy garment edges sometimes use a chainless foundation, but for everyday flat work the foundation chain is where you begin.
